title: Structure, Naming & Stereochemistry
description: Hybridization, resonance, acidity and pKa, functional groups, IUPAC names, conformations and chairs, chirality, R/S and E/Z, enantiomers, diastereomers and meso compounds, and IR and NMR basics.

cards.title: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen atom in pyridine, $\ce{C5H5N}$?
cards.body:
$sp^2$

The nitrogen is part of the flat aromatic ring and adds one electron to the $\pi$ system from its $p$ orbital. Its **lone pair** sits in an $sp^2$ orbital in the plane of the ring, outside the aromatic sextet.

Key idea: that lone pair isn't needed for aromaticity, so pyridine is a base (its conjugate acid has $\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 5.2$).
Watch out: in **pyrrole**, the nitrogen's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, so pyrrole is a very weak base.
cards.searchQuery: pyridine nitrogen hybridization sp2 lone pair aromatic

cards.title: What is the ideal bond angle (in degrees) around an sp2 carbon such as the carbons of ethene?
cards.body:
120

Three σ domains spread out in a **trigonal planar** arrangement. The unhybridized p orbital sits perpendicular to that plane and forms the π bond.

Example: in ethene all six atoms lie in one plane with H–C–H and H–C=C angles near 120°.
cards.searchQuery: sp2 carbon bond angle trigonal planar 120

cards.title: How many σ bonds are in propene, $\ce{CH3CH=CH2}$?
cards.body:
8

Six C–H σ bonds, one C–C σ bond, and the σ component of the C=C double bond. The double bond also holds **one π bond**, so there is 1 π bond in total.

Tip: a double bond is 1 σ + 1 π; a triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π.
cards.searchQuery: count sigma and pi bonds propene

cards.title: Why is rotation about a C=C double bond restricted at room temperature?
cards.body:
Rotating would break the π bond.

The π bond needs the two p orbitals to be **parallel**. A 90° twist removes their overlap, which costs roughly 60-65 kcal/mol, far more than thermal energy provides.

Key idea: restricted rotation is what makes E/Z (cis/trans) isomers separable.
cards.searchQuery: pi bond restricted rotation cis trans alkene

cards.title: Rank the carbon-carbon bonds from shortest to longest: single, double, triple.
cards.body:
Triple < double < single

Typical lengths: C≡C about 120 pm, C=C about 134 pm, C–C about 154 pm. More bonding electron density pulls the nuclei closer.

Watch out: the strongest bond is also the shortest, but each added π bond adds less strength than the first σ bond.
cards.searchQuery: carbon carbon bond length single double triple

cards.title: What is the hybridization of the positively charged carbon in a simple carbocation such as $\ce{(CH3)3C+}$?
cards.body:
sp2

Three σ bonds, no lone pair, so the cationic carbon is **trigonal planar**. The empty p orbital is perpendicular to the plane and is the electrophilic site.

Why: this planar geometry lets a nucleophile attack from either face, which is why $\mathrm{S_N1}$ gives racemization.
cards.searchQuery: carbocation hybridization sp2 empty p orbital

cards.title: The nitrogen of an amide is closer to sp2 than sp3. Why?
cards.body:
Its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O.

Resonance puts partial double-bond character in the C–N bond, so the nitrogen is **planar** and its lone pair sits in a p orbital aligned with the carbonyl π system.

Example: this is why amides are far less basic than amines and rotate slowly about the C–N bond.
cards.searchQuery: amide nitrogen sp2 resonance planar

cards.title: What is the hybridization of the central carbon in allene, $\ce{CH2=C=CH2}$?
cards.body:
sp

The central carbon has two double bonds (two σ domains), so it is **linear**. The two terminal carbons are sp2.

Watch out: the two π bonds use perpendicular p orbitals, so the two $\ce{CH2}$ planes are twisted 90° to each other.
cards.searchQuery: allene central carbon sp hybridization

cards.title: What is the C–O bond order in each C–O bond of the acetate ion, $\ce{CH3COO-}$?
cards.body:
1.5

The two resonance forms are equivalent, so the negative charge is shared equally. Both C–O bonds are identical in length, between a single and a double bond.

Key idea: the real structure is a **resonance hybrid**, not a rapid flipping between contributors.
cards.searchQuery: acetate ion resonance hybrid bond order 1.5

cards.title: When drawing resonance structures, what may move and what must stay fixed?
cards.body:
Only electrons (π and lone pairs) move; atom positions stay fixed.

All contributors must have the same atoms connected the same way and the same net charge. Moving an atom or a σ bond makes an isomer, not a resonance form.

Watch out: the double-headed arrow ↔ means resonance; equilibrium arrows ⇌ mean separate species.
cards.searchQuery: resonance structures rules electrons move atoms fixed

cards.title: Which resonance contributor is generally more important: one where every atom has a full octet, or one with an incomplete octet on carbon?
cards.body:
The one with full octets.

Other things that make a contributor more significant:
- more covalent bonds
- fewer formal charges
- negative charge on the more electronegative atom

Example: for a protonated carbonyl, the form with $\ce{C+}$ and a neutral O has an incomplete octet, but the oxonium form ($\ce{C=OH+}$) has full octets and dominates.
cards.searchQuery: major resonance contributor octet rule formal charge

cards.title: In the allyl cation $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2+}$, which carbon(s) carry the positive charge?
cards.body:
C1 and C3 (the two terminal carbons), each about half.

The resonance forms $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2+ <-> +CH2-CH=CH2}$ are equivalent. The central carbon carries essentially no positive charge.

Why: this delocalization is why allylic cations are about as stable as secondary carbocations.
cards.searchQuery: allyl cation resonance charge terminal carbons

cards.title: What is the approximate pKa of acetic acid? (one decimal is fine)
cards.body:
4.76

The acetate ion is stabilized by **resonance** over two oxygens, so acetic acid ionizes far more readily than an alcohol.

Tip: carboxylic acids sit around pKa 4-5; memorize 4.76 as the benchmark.
cards.searchQuery: acetic acid pKa 4.76

cards.title: What is the approximate pKa of a terminal alkyne C–H, such as the one in propyne?
cards.body:
25

The sp carbon is 50% s character, so the lone pair of the acetylide sits closer to the nucleus and is more stable than an sp2 (pKa about 44) or sp3 (about 50) carbanion.

Example: alkyne 25 < ammonia 38 < alkene 44 < alkane 50.
cards.searchQuery: terminal alkyne pKa 25 acidity sp hybridization

cards.title: What is the approximate pKa of phenol?
cards.body:
10

Phenoxide's negative charge delocalizes into the ring (ortho and para carbons), so phenol is about **million-fold more acidic than cyclohexanol** (pKa about 16-18).

Watch out: phenol is still a much weaker acid than a carboxylic acid; it dissolves in NaOH but not in $\ce{NaHCO3}$.
cards.searchQuery: phenol pKa 10 phenoxide resonance

cards.title: What is the pKa of water (as an acid, ignoring the 55.5 M concentration factor)? Give the commonly quoted value.
cards.body:
15.7

This is the pKa of $\ce{H2O}$ losing a proton to give $\ce{HO-}$. It is close to simple alcohols (about 16), so hydroxide and alkoxides have similar basicity.

Watch out: do not confuse it with 14, which is $\mathrm{p}K_w$.
cards.searchQuery: pKa of water 15.7 versus pKw 14

cards.title: What does the mnemonic ARIO stand for when comparing acidity of H–A bonds?
cards.body:
Atom, Resonance, Induction, Orbital.

These are the factors that stabilize the conjugate base A⁻, in priority order:
1. **Atom**: the atom bearing the charge (size and electronegativity)
2. **Resonance**: delocalization of the charge
3. **Induction**: nearby electron-withdrawing groups
4. **Orbital**: more s character holds the charge better

Mnemonic: ARIO, apply in that order.
cards.searchQuery: ARIO acidity trends atom resonance induction orbital

cards.title: Rank the C–H acidity of ethane, ethene and ethyne from most to least acidic, and give the reason.
cards.body:
Ethyne > ethene > ethane.

The conjugate base's lone pair is held in an sp (50% s), sp2 (33% s) or sp3 (25% s) orbital. **More s character** means the electrons are closer to the nucleus and more stable.

Watch out: this is an orbital effect, not a resonance effect.
cards.searchQuery: acidity alkane alkene alkyne s character

cards.title: In an acid-base reaction, which side does the equilibrium favor?
cards.body:
The side with the weaker acid (and weaker base).

Compare the pKa of the acid on each side: the reaction goes toward the higher pKa. A difference of $n$ pKa units gives $K \approx 10^{n}$.

Example: acetic acid (4.76) with ethoxide (conjugate acid pKa about 16) goes essentially to completion, since the products' acid is much weaker.
cards.searchQuery: acid base equilibrium favors weaker acid pKa comparison

cards.title: Which common strong base (give the formula) can fully deprotonate a terminal alkyne, but $\ce{NaOH}$ cannot?
cards.body:
NaNH2

The conjugate acid $\ce{NH3}$ has pKa about 38, well above the alkyne's 25, so the equilibrium lies far to the acetylide. Hydroxide's conjugate acid (water, 15.7) is a much stronger acid than the alkyne, so $\ce{NaOH}$ barely deprotonates it.

Tip: the base's conjugate acid must have a pKa higher than the acid you want to deprotonate.
cards.searchQuery: NaNH2 deprotonate terminal alkyne acetylide

cards.title: Name the functional group in $\ce{CH3CONH2}$.
cards.body:
amide

A carbonyl carbon bonded directly to nitrogen. Amides are the **least reactive** common carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution.

Watch out: an amine has no C=O; an amide always does.
cards.searchQuery: amide functional group carbonyl nitrogen

cards.title: Name the functional group in $\ce{(CH3CO)2O}$.
cards.body:
Acid anhydride

Two acyl groups share one oxygen, $\ce{R-CO-O-CO-R}$. This one is acetic anhydride.

Key idea: anhydrides are the second most reactive acid derivatives, after acyl chlorides, and they readily acylate alcohols and amines.
cards.searchQuery: acid anhydride functional group acetic anhydride structure

cards.title: Name the functional group in $\ce{CH3COCl}$.
cards.body:
acyl chloride

Also called an acid chloride: $\ce{R-C(=O)Cl}$. It is the **most reactive** carboxylic acid derivative because chloride is an excellent leaving group and offers no resonance donation to the C=O.

Example: this compound is ethanoyl (acetyl) chloride.
cards.searchQuery: acyl chloride acid chloride functional group

cards.title: Is 2-propanol a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol?
cards.body:
secondary

Alcohol class depends on how many **carbons** are attached to the carbon bearing the OH. In $\ce{(CH3)2CHOH}$ that carbon has two carbon neighbors.

Watch out: classify by the carbon bonded to OH, not by the number of substituents on the oxygen.
cards.searchQuery: primary secondary tertiary alcohol classification

cards.title: Is $\ce{(CH3)3N}$ a primary, secondary or tertiary amine?
cards.body:
tertiary

Amine class counts the **carbon groups on nitrogen**: one is primary, two secondary, three tertiary.

Watch out: this differs from alcohols and alkyl halides, where the class refers to the carbon bearing the functional group.
cards.searchQuery: classify amines primary secondary tertiary nitrogen

cards.title: What structural feature distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.body:
An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon bears at least one hydrogen.

Aldehydes are $\ce{R-CHO}$, with the carbonyl at the end of a chain; ketones are $\ce{R-CO-R'}$ with two carbon groups on the carbonyl carbon.

Why: that H is why aldehydes oxidize easily to carboxylic acids while ketones resist oxidation.
cards.searchQuery: aldehyde versus ketone structure difference

cards.title: Give the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3}$.
cards.body:
2,3-Dimethylpentane

The longest chain has five carbons. Numbering from the left puts the methyls at $2$ and $3$, lower than $3$ and $4$ from the right.

Watch out: two identical substituents need the prefix **di-** and a locant for each one.
Example: C3 carries H, a methyl, an ethyl and an isopropyl group, so it is a stereocenter and the compound is chiral.
cards.searchQuery: 2,3-dimethylpentane IUPAC naming branched alkane

cards.title: Give the IUPAC name of $\ce{(CH3)3CCH2CH(CH3)2}$.
cards.body:
2,2,4-Trimethylpentane

The longest chain has five carbons. Numbering from the end nearer the branches gives methyls at $2$, $2$ and $4$, lower than $2$, $4$, $4$ from the other end.

Example: this is **isooctane**, the standard with an octane rating of $100$.
Watch out: give every substituent its own locant, even two on the same carbon (2,2-).
cards.searchQuery: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane IUPAC name isooctane

cards.title: Give the IUPAC name of $\ce{(CH3)3CCH2CH3}$.
cards.body:
2,2-dimethylbutane

Longest chain: 4 carbons. Both methyls sit on the same carbon, and numbering from the end nearest them gives locants 2,2 (not 3,3). Repeat the locant for each substituent.

Tip: two identical substituents need the prefix **di-** and a locant for each, separated by commas.
cards.searchQuery: 2,2-dimethylbutane IUPAC naming neohexane

cards.title: When two numbering directions both seem valid for the parent chain, how do you choose?
cards.body:
Choose the direction giving the lowest locant at the first point of difference.

Compare the full set of locants term by term, not their sum. For example, locants {2,3,6} beat {2,5,6} because 3 is less than 5 at the first difference.

Key idea: functional group suffix first, then multiple bonds, then substituents, with alphabetical order as the last tiebreaker.
cards.searchQuery: IUPAC lowest locant first point of difference rule

cards.title: Name $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH(CH2CH3)CH2CH3}$.
cards.body:
3-ethyl-2-methylpentane

Parent chain: pentane. Substituents are listed **alphabetically** (ethyl before methyl), each with its locant. Numbering from the methyl end gives {2,3}, lower than {3,4} from the other end.

Watch out: the multiplying prefixes di- and tri- are ignored when alphabetizing, so dimethyl sorts under m.
cards.searchQuery: alphabetical order substituents 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane

cards.title: Name $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH3}$ (IUPAC).
cards.body:
1-butene

Number the chain so the **double bond gets the lowest locant**; the locant goes before the stem (1-butene) or inside it (but-1-ene, current IUPAC style).

Example: $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$ is 2-butene, which exists as E and Z isomers; 1-butene has none.
cards.searchQuery: 1-butene IUPAC name alkene numbering

cards.title: Name $\ce{CH3C#CCH3}$ (IUPAC).
cards.body:
2-butyne

The triple bond sits between C2 and C3 of a four-carbon chain. Alkynes use the suffix **-yne**, and the locant is the lower carbon number of the bond.

Example: the isomer $\ce{HC#CCH2CH3}$ is 1-butyne, a terminal alkyne (pKa about 25).
cards.searchQuery: 2-butyne IUPAC name internal alkyne

cards.title: Give the IUPAC name of $\ce{(CH3)2CHOH}$ (not the common name).
cards.body:
2-propanol

Drop the -e of the alkane and add **-ol**, with the locant for the OH: propan-2-ol (current style) or 2-propanol.

Watch out: isopropyl alcohol is the common name, not the IUPAC name.
cards.searchQuery: 2-propanol propan-2-ol IUPAC alcohol naming

cards.title: Name $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2COCH3}$. (Which group gets the suffix?)
cards.body:
4-hydroxy-2-pentanone

The ketone outranks the alcohol, so the ketone takes the suffix **-one** and the OH becomes the prefix **hydroxy-**. Number to give the ketone the lowest locant (2).

Tip: suffix priority runs acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene > alkyne.
cards.searchQuery: functional group priority naming ketone hydroxy IUPAC

cards.title: What is the common name of the substituent $\ce{-CH(CH3)CH2CH3}$?
cards.body:
sec-Butyl

It attaches through the **second** carbon of a four-carbon chain, which is a secondary carbon.

Example: 2-bromobutane is also called sec-butyl bromide.
Tip: the four butyl groups are butyl $\ce{-CH2CH2CH2CH3}$, sec-butyl, isobutyl $\ce{-CH2CH(CH3)2}$ and tert-butyl $\ce{-C(CH3)3}$.
cards.searchQuery: sec-butyl group structure alkyl substituent names

cards.title: What is the name of the substituent $\ce{C6H5CH2-}$?
cards.body:
benzyl

A benzyl group is a $\ce{CH2}$ attached to a phenyl ring. Do not confuse it with **phenyl**, which is $\ce{C6H5-}$ bonded directly.

Why it matters: benzylic cations and radicals are resonance-stabilized, so benzylic positions are especially reactive.
cards.searchQuery: benzyl group versus phenyl group

cards.title: On a benzene ring, what is the term for substituents in a 1,3 relationship?
cards.body:
meta

Ortho is 1,2; meta is 1,3; para is 1,4.

Example: 1,3-dichlorobenzene is m-dichlorobenzene.

Tip: the same prefixes tell you which positions an incoming electrophile prefers in aromatic substitution.
cards.searchQuery: ortho meta para benzene substituent positions

cards.title: Name the cyclohexane with Cl and $\ce{CH3}$ on adjacent carbons (ignore stereochemistry).
cards.body:
1-chloro-2-methylcyclohexane

On a ring there is no suffix to anchor numbering, so the locants tie at {1,2}. **Alphabetical order** breaks the tie: chloro comes before methyl, so Cl gets C1.

Watch out: do not number the way that puts the smaller group at 1; alphabetical order decides.
cards.searchQuery: name substituted cyclohexane alphabetical numbering chloro methyl

cards.title: Name $\ce{CH3CH2COOH}$ (IUPAC).
cards.body:
propanoic acid

The carboxyl carbon is always C1, so no locant is needed. Replace -e of the alkane with **-oic acid**.

Example: the common name is propionic acid; $\ce{CH3COOH}$ is ethanoic (acetic) acid.
cards.searchQuery: propanoic acid IUPAC carboxylic acid naming

cards.title: About how large is the rotational energy barrier of ethane, in kcal/mol (staggered to eclipsed)?
cards.body:
3

The eclipsed conformer is about 3 kcal/mol (roughly 12 kJ/mol) higher than the staggered one. This is **torsional strain** from eclipsing C–H bonds, with three H/H eclipsing interactions of about 1 kcal/mol each.

Watch out: the barrier is small, so ethane rotates freely at room temperature.
cards.searchQuery: ethane rotational barrier staggered eclipsed kcal/mol

cards.title: In a staggered conformation, what is the dihedral angle (in degrees) between a front and the nearest back substituent in a Newman projection?
cards.body:
60

In a staggered conformer each front bond sits midway between two back bonds, 60° from each. In an eclipsed conformer the angle is 0° (or 120°).

Tip: in butane, anti is 180° and gauche is 60°.
cards.searchQuery: staggered conformation dihedral angle 60 Newman projection

cards.title: Rank the conformers of butane (about the C2–C3 bond) from most to least stable.
cards.body:
Anti > gauche > eclipsed (CH3/H) > fully eclipsed (CH3/CH3).

Anti puts the two methyls at 180°. Gauche (60°) is about 0.9 kcal/mol higher due to steric strain. The **fully eclipsed** form is the energy maximum, roughly 4.5–6 kcal/mol above anti (textbooks differ).

Watch out: staggered conformers are minima, eclipsed ones are maxima.
cards.searchQuery: butane conformations anti gauche eclipsed energy diagram

cards.title: By about how many kcal/mol is gauche butane higher in energy than anti butane?
cards.body:
0.9

The two methyl groups are 60° apart and crowd each other. That steric repulsion is called **gauche interaction** strain.

Example: at room temperature, roughly 70% of butane molecules are anti and 30% gauche.
cards.searchQuery: gauche butane energy 0.9 kcal/mol steric strain

cards.title: What is the difference between torsional strain and steric strain?
cards.body:
Torsional strain comes from eclipsed bonds; steric strain comes from atoms forced too close together.

Torsional strain is relieved by rotating to a staggered arrangement. **Steric strain** (as in gauche butane or 1,3-diaxial interactions) comes from non-bonded repulsion.

Key idea: ring strain combines angle strain, torsional strain and steric strain.
cards.searchQuery: torsional strain versus steric strain definition

cards.title: What is the most stable conformation of cyclohexane?
cards.body:
chair

The chair has nearly perfect 109.5° angles and **all bonds staggered**, so it has essentially no angle or torsional strain.

Why: other conformers (boat, twist-boat, half-chair) have eclipsing or flagpole strain, and are higher by 5.5 kcal/mol or more.
cards.searchQuery: cyclohexane chair conformation most stable

cards.title: What is the C–C–C bond angle in cyclopropane, and why is the ring strained?
cards.body:
60°, far from the ideal 109.5°.

The bent "banana" bonds overlap poorly, creating large **angle strain**. The C–H bonds are also fully eclipsed, adding torsional strain. Total strain is about 27.5 kcal/mol.

Why it matters: this strain makes cyclopropane and epoxides prone to ring-opening.
cards.searchQuery: cyclopropane angle strain 60 degrees ring strain

cards.title: Why is a substituent on a cyclohexane chair usually more stable in the equatorial position than the axial one?
cards.body:
Axial substituents suffer 1,3-diaxial interactions.

An axial group sits close to the two other axial hydrogens on the same side of the ring (carbons 3 and 5 relative to it). Equatorial groups point outward and avoid this crowding.

Example: axial methylcyclohexane is about 1.7 kcal/mol less stable than equatorial.
cards.searchQuery: axial equatorial substituent 1,3-diaxial interaction cyclohexane

cards.title: What happens to an axial substituent when a cyclohexane chair undergoes a ring flip?
cards.body:
It becomes equatorial.

All axial groups become equatorial and vice versa. The relative cis/trans relationship of substituents does **not** change.

Watch out: a ring flip is a conformational change (bond rotations), not a configurational one.
cards.searchQuery: chair flip ring flip axial equatorial interconversion

cards.title: What is the approximate A value of a methyl group on cyclohexane, in kcal/mol?
cards.body:
1.7

The A value is the free-energy preference for the **equatorial** position over axial. Larger groups have larger A values: ethyl about 1.8, isopropyl about 2.2, tert-butyl about 5.

Tip: a bigger A value means a stronger preference for equatorial.
cards.searchQuery: A value methyl cyclohexane 1.7 kcal/mol equatorial preference

cards.title: Why is a cyclohexane bearing a tert-butyl group essentially locked in one chair conformation?
cards.body:
Axial tert-butyl is far too crowded (A value about 5 kcal/mol).

The flipped chair would put the bulky $\ce{C(CH3)3}$ axial with severe 1,3-diaxial interactions, so over 99.9% of molecules keep it **equatorial**.

Example: chemists use tert-butyl as a conformational "anchor" to study cis and trans isomers.
cards.searchQuery: tert-butyl cyclohexane locked conformation anchor group

cards.title: What are the positions of the two methyls in the more stable chair of trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane?
cards.body:
Both equatorial (diequatorial).

In a trans-1,4 pattern the groups are either both equatorial or both axial, and the ring flip interconverts them. Diequatorial is far more stable (about 3.4 kcal/mol, twice the methyl A value).

Tip: trans-1,4 and cis-1,3 can be diequatorial; cis-1,4 and trans-1,3 are always axial/equatorial.
cards.searchQuery: trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane diequatorial chair conformer

cards.title: In the more stable chair of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane, how are the two methyl groups positioned?
cards.body:
Both equatorial (diequatorial).

For 1,3 substituents, cis means both equatorial or both axial. The diequatorial chair avoids a severe 1,3-diaxial methyl/methyl clash, so it dominates.

Watch out: the trans-1,3 isomer cannot be diequatorial; it is always axial/equatorial.
cards.searchQuery: cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane diequatorial more stable chair

cards.title: How many of the 12 hydrogens on a cyclohexane chair are axial?
cards.body:
6

Each carbon has one axial and one equatorial position, so there are 6 axial H and 6 equatorial H. Axial positions alternate **up and down** around the ring.

Example: adjacent carbons have axial bonds pointing in opposite directions, which is why trans-1,2 groups can be diaxial.
cards.searchQuery: cyclohexane chair six axial hydrogens

cards.title: Why is the boat conformation of cyclohexane less stable than the chair?
cards.body:
It has eclipsed bonds and a flagpole interaction.

The four carbons in the base of the boat have eclipsed C–H bonds (torsional strain), and the two "flagpole" hydrogens point at each other (steric strain). The twist-boat relieves some of this.

Key idea: the boat lies about 6.9 kcal/mol above the chair; the slightly lower-energy **twist-boat** is the real intermediate in ring flipping.
cards.searchQuery: boat conformation cyclohexane flagpole interaction eclipsing

cards.title: What is the term for an sp3 carbon bonded to four different groups?
cards.body:
stereocenter

Also called a **chirality center** or stereogenic center. Swapping any two groups on it gives a different stereoisomer.

Watch out: "different" is judged on the whole group, not just the first atom. Two carbon chains can differ only farther from the center.
cards.searchQuery: stereocenter chirality center four different groups

cards.title: Is 3-pentanol chiral? (yes or no)
cards.body:
no

C3 bears H, OH and **two identical ethyl groups**, so it is not a stereocenter. The molecule has a mirror plane through C3 and is achiral.

Example: by contrast, 2-pentanol has four different groups on C2 (H, OH, $\ce{CH3}$, propyl) and is chiral.
cards.searchQuery: 3-pentanol achiral no stereocenter identical groups

cards.title: Which is chiral: 2-butanol or 2-propanol?
cards.body:
2-Butanol

In 2-butanol, C2 carries four different groups (H, OH, $\ce{CH3}$ and $\ce{CH2CH3}$), so it is a **stereocenter** and the molecule is chiral. In 2-propanol, C2 carries two identical methyl groups, so the molecule is achiral.

Tip: look for an $sp^3$ carbon with four different groups; any two identical groups rule it out.
cards.searchQuery: why 2-butanol is chiral and 2-propanol is not stereocenter

cards.title: Which has the higher CIP priority: vinyl ($\ce{-CH=CH2}$) or isopropyl ($\ce{-CH(CH3)2}$)?
cards.body:
vinyl

Both start with (C, C, H) because the double bond's second carbon is **duplicated**. At the next sphere, the vinyl branches are {(C, H, H), (0, 0, 0)} while isopropyl's are {(H, H, H), (H, H, H)}, and (C, H, H) beats (H, H, H).

Watch out: a duplicated atom carries only phantom substituents (atomic number 0).
cards.searchQuery: CIP priority vinyl versus isopropyl duplicate atoms

cards.title: What is the maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with 3 stereocenters?
cards.body:
8

The maximum is $2^n$ for $n$ stereocenters, so $2^3 = 8$. Meso forms or other symmetry can make the actual number **smaller**.

Watch out: this is a ceiling, not a guarantee; for example, tartaric acid has only 3 stereoisomers, not 4.
cards.searchQuery: maximum number stereoisomers 2^n stereocenters

cards.title: How do the physical properties of two enantiomers compare in an achiral environment?
cards.body:
They are identical, except that they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.

Melting point, boiling point, density and solubility match. Differences appear only with **chiral** reagents, enzymes or receptors.

Example: (R)-carvone smells like spearmint and (S)-carvone like caraway because olfactory receptors are chiral.
cards.searchQuery: enantiomers identical physical properties optical rotation opposite

cards.title: What are diastereomers, and how do their physical properties compare?
cards.body:
Stereoisomers that are not mirror images; their physical properties differ.

Because they have different energies and shapes, diastereomers have different melting points, boiling points and solubilities, so they can be separated by ordinary methods such as crystallization or chromatography.

Key idea: enantiomers need a chiral resolving agent; diastereomers do not.
cards.searchQuery: diastereomers definition different physical properties separation

cards.title: What is a meso compound?
cards.body:
An achiral compound that contains stereocenters.

It has an **internal plane of symmetry** (or inversion center) that makes it superimposable on its mirror image. Its stereocenters have opposite configurations that cancel, e.g. (2R,3S).

Watch out: meso compounds are optically inactive even though they are a single pure compound.
cards.searchQuery: meso compound definition internal plane of symmetry stereocenters

cards.title: How many stereoisomers does tartaric acid, $\ce{HOOC-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-COOH}$, have?
cards.body:
3

The two stereocenters would give 4, but the structure is symmetric. The stereoisomers are the (R,R) and (S,S) enantiomers and the achiral **meso** (R,S) form.

Example: the meso form is optically inactive and is a diastereomer of both chiral forms.
cards.searchQuery: tartaric acid three stereoisomers meso

cards.title: Is (2R,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane chiral? (yes or no)
cards.body:
no

The molecule has identical ends, so (2R,3S) has a mirror plane in its eclipsed conformation and is **meso**. Its mirror image is itself.

Watch out: (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) are the chiral pair; opposite descriptors on a symmetric molecule signal meso.
cards.searchQuery: meso 2,3-dichlorobutane 2R 3S achiral

cards.title: What is a racemic mixture, and what is its optical rotation?
cards.body:
A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers; its optical rotation is zero.

The equal and opposite rotations cancel. It is written (±) or dl, and has an ee of 0%.

Example: $\mathrm{S_N1}$ reactions at a stereocenter typically give racemic products because the planar carbocation is attacked from both faces.
cards.searchQuery: racemic mixture 50:50 enantiomers optical rotation zero

cards.title: A mixture is 75% (R) and 25% (S). What is the enantiomeric excess (ee), in percent?
cards.body:
50

$\mathrm{ee} = |\%R - \%S| = 75 - 25 = 50\%$. Equivalently, the mixture behaves as 50% pure (R) plus 50% racemate.

Tip: the observed rotation of the mixture is 50% of the pure (R) value.
cards.searchQuery: enantiomeric excess calculation 75% R 25% S

cards.title: (R)-2-butanol has a specific rotation of about $-13.5^\circ$. What is the specific rotation of pure (S)-2-butanol, as a number?
cards.body:
+13.5

Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by **equal magnitudes in opposite directions**. The sign is an experimental property.

Watch out: there is no simple rule linking R/S labels to the sign (+ or −) of rotation; it must be measured.
cards.searchQuery: enantiomers specific rotation equal opposite 2-butanol

cards.title: The lowest-priority group points toward you, and priorities 1 to 2 to 3 run clockwise. What is the configuration (R or S)?
cards.body:
S

Clockwise would be R if the lowest group pointed **away**. With it toward you, the apparent direction is reversed, so the true configuration is the opposite.

Tip: when the lowest priority is on a horizontal wedge or toward you, read the direction and flip the answer.
cards.searchQuery: R S assignment lowest priority toward viewer reverse

cards.title: Does the R or S label tell you whether a compound is dextrorotatory (+) or levorotatory (−)?
cards.body:
No.

R/S describes the three-dimensional arrangement using CIP priorities, whereas (+) and (−) are **measured** rotation directions. They have no fixed correlation.

Example: (R)-lactic acid is the (−) form, but other R compounds are (+).
cards.searchQuery: R S configuration versus optical rotation sign no correlation

cards.title: In a Fischer projection, which way do the horizontal and vertical bonds point?
cards.body:
Horizontal toward the viewer; vertical away from the viewer.

The carbon chain runs vertically with the most oxidized carbon on top. Each stereocenter is a crossing point.

Watch out: a Fischer projection must not be rotated 90° in the plane, which would invert every center.
cards.searchQuery: Fischer projection horizontal toward viewer vertical away

cards.title: In a Fischer projection, what does swapping two substituents on a stereocenter do to its configuration?
cards.body:
It inverts it (R becomes S, or S becomes R).

One swap inverts; two swaps restore the original. Rotating the whole projection **180° in the plane** keeps the configuration.

Tip: to find R/S from a Fischer projection, if the lowest-priority group is on a horizontal bond, determine the direction and reverse it.
cards.searchQuery: Fischer projection swapping substituents inversion configuration

cards.title: Is (Z)-2-butene the cis or trans isomer?
cards.body:
cis

In Z (German zusammen, "together"), the **higher-priority groups** on each alkene carbon lie on the same side. Here those are the two methyls.

Watch out: cis/trans and E/Z often agree for simple alkenes, but E/Z uses CIP priorities and is the only system valid for fully substituted alkenes.
cards.searchQuery: Z alkene cis zusammen 2-butene E/Z

cards.title: In $\ce{BrCH=CHCl}$ the Br and Cl are on the same side of the double bond. Is it E or Z?
cards.body:
Z

On each carbon the halogen outranks hydrogen (Br > H, Cl > H). Both high-priority groups are on the same side, so the alkene is **Z**.

Example: if Br and Cl were on opposite sides, it would be E (German entgegen, "opposite").
cards.searchQuery: E Z designation 1-bromo-2-chloroethene CIP priority

cards.title: Does 2-methyl-2-butene, $\ce{(CH3)2C=CHCH3}$, have E and Z isomers? (yes or no)
cards.body:
no

E/Z isomerism needs **two different groups on each sp2 carbon**. C2 bears two identical methyl groups, so swapping them produces the same molecule.

Example: 2-butene qualifies because each sp2 carbon has H and $\ce{CH3}$.
cards.searchQuery: E Z isomerism requirement two different groups 2-methyl-2-butene

cards.title: How many stereoisomers does 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane have?
cards.body:
3

The cis isomer is **meso** (a single achiral compound), and the trans isomer exists as a pair of enantiomers: 1 + 2 = 3.

Why: the cis compound has a mirror plane in its planar depiction, and chair flipping rapidly interconverts its two chiral-looking forms.
cards.searchQuery: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane stereoisomers cis meso trans enantiomers

cards.title: How many stereoisomers does 1,4-dimethylcyclohexane have?
cards.body:
2

Only cis and trans. Both are **achiral**, because each has a mirror plane through C1 and C4, and there are no enantiomers.

Watch out: two stereocenters do not always mean four stereoisomers; here neither carbon is a true stereocenter.
cards.searchQuery: 1,4-dimethylcyclohexane cis trans stereoisomers achiral

cards.title: Which is chiral: cis- or trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane?
cards.body:
trans

The trans isomer has no internal mirror plane and exists as a pair of enantiomers, (1R,2R) and (1S,2S). The cis isomer is meso.

Tip: for 1,2-disubstituted rings with identical substituents, trans is chiral and cis is meso.
cards.searchQuery: trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane chiral enantiomers

cards.title: How do constitutional isomers differ from stereoisomers?
cards.body:
Constitutional isomers have different connectivity; stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different 3D arrangement.

Example: butane and 2-methylpropane are constitutional isomers ($\ce{C4H10}$). cis- and trans-2-butene are stereoisomers.

Key idea: stereoisomers split into enantiomers and diastereomers.
cards.searchQuery: constitutional isomers versus stereoisomers difference

cards.title: A compound is (2R,3S,4R). What are the descriptors of its enantiomer? (format: 2X,3X,4X)
cards.body:
2S,3R,4S

An enantiomer is the mirror image, so **every** stereocenter is inverted. A diastereomer would have only some centers inverted.

Watch out: the locants stay the same; only R and S switch.
cards.searchQuery: enantiomer descriptors invert all stereocenters R S

cards.title: An alcohol O–H stretch appears as a strong, broad IR band centered near what wavenumber (cm⁻¹)?
cards.body:
3300

The range is roughly 3200-3600 cm⁻¹. The band is **broad** because of hydrogen bonding.

Watch out: an N–H stretch falls in the same region but is sharper and weaker.
cards.searchQuery: IR alcohol O-H stretch broad 3300 wavenumber

cards.title: At about what wavenumber (cm⁻¹) does the C=O stretch of a simple ketone appear?
cards.body:
1715

The C=O stretch is a **strong, sharp** band that is easy to spot. Simple aldehydes absorb near 1730, esters near 1735, and carboxylic acids near 1710.

Tip: memorize 1715 as the reference point, then shift up or down for the carbonyl type.
cards.searchQuery: IR ketone C=O stretch 1715 wavenumber

cards.title: What does the O–H stretch of a carboxylic acid look like in an IR spectrum?
cards.body:
A very broad band spanning about 2500-3300 cm⁻¹.

Strong hydrogen bonding in the acid **dimer** smears the O–H band, and it often overlaps the C–H stretches. A C=O peak near 1710 cm⁻¹ accompanies it.

Tip: broad enough to "swallow" the C–H region means carboxylic acid.
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid IR O-H very broad 2500-3300

cards.title: At about what wavenumber (cm⁻¹) does the $\ce{C#N}$ stretch of a nitrile appear?
cards.body:
2250

The triple-bond region (2100-2260 cm⁻¹) is otherwise quiet. A nitrile band is sharp and medium in intensity.

Watch out: an alkyne C≡C is near 2100-2260 as well but may be absent for symmetrical alkynes.
cards.searchQuery: IR nitrile C#N stretch 2250 wavenumber

cards.title: At about what wavenumber (cm⁻¹) is the C=O stretch of a saturated ester?
cards.body:
1735

Esters absorb about 20 cm⁻¹ higher than ketones because the ester oxygen's inductive effect strengthens the C=O.

Example: amides absorb lower, near 1650, because nitrogen's resonance donation weakens the C=O.
cards.searchQuery: IR ester C=O stretch 1735 wavenumber

cards.title: How do primary and secondary amines differ in the IR N–H stretching region?
cards.body:
A primary amine shows two N–H bands; a secondary amine shows one.

The two bands of $\ce{R-NH2}$ come from symmetric and asymmetric stretching. A tertiary amine has no N–H, so no band.

Watch out: both are sharper and weaker than the broad O–H of an alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: IR primary secondary amine N-H stretch two bands one band

cards.title: Which side of 3000 cm⁻¹ do sp3 C–H and sp2 C–H stretches appear on?
cards.body:
sp3 C–H just below 3000; sp2 C–H just above 3000.

A terminal alkyne ≡C–H gives a sharp band near 3300 cm⁻¹. More s character gives a stronger, higher-frequency bond.

Tip: a weak band just above 3000 suggests an alkene or aromatic ring.
cards.searchQuery: IR C-H stretch sp3 below 3000 sp2 above 3000

cards.title: How does conjugation of a C=O with a C=C or aromatic ring affect its IR stretching frequency?
cards.body:
It lowers it, by about 20-40 cm⁻¹.

Resonance gives the carbonyl some single-bond character, so the bond is slightly weaker. Acetophenone absorbs near 1685 cm⁻¹ compared with 1715 for acetone.

Key idea: electron donation by resonance lowers C=O frequency; induction from electronegative groups raises it.
cards.searchQuery: conjugation lowers carbonyl IR frequency acetophenone 1685

cards.title: In the $^1$H NMR of an ethyl group $\ce{-CH2CH3}$ attached to an electronegative atom, what is the splitting of the $\ce{CH3}$ signal?
cards.body:
triplet

By the **n + 1 rule**, the $\ce{CH3}$ sees two neighboring H on the $\ce{CH2}$, giving 2 + 1 = 3 lines (1:2:1). The $\ce{CH2}$ sees three H and is a quartet.

Tip: a quartet plus a triplet with 2H:3H integration is the classic ethyl fingerprint.
cards.searchQuery: NMR ethyl group triplet quartet n+1 rule

cards.title: In the $^1$H NMR of an isopropyl group, what is the splitting pattern of the lone $\ce{CH}$ proton?
cards.body:
septet

It sees six equivalent neighboring protons (two methyls), so 6 + 1 = 7 lines. The methyls appear as a 6H doublet.

Example: a 6H doublet plus a 1H septet indicates $\ce{-CH(CH3)2}$.
cards.searchQuery: NMR isopropyl septet doublet n+1 rule

cards.title: What does the integration (area) of a $^1$H NMR signal tell you?
cards.body:
The relative number of equivalent hydrogens giving that signal.

Integrals are ratios, not absolute counts. A 3:2 ratio could be 3H and 2H, or 6H and 4H.

Tip: use the molecular formula to scale the ratio to the real number of hydrogens.
cards.searchQuery: NMR integration relative number of hydrogens signal area

cards.title: Approximately what chemical shift (ppm) does an aldehyde proton $\ce{R-CHO}$ show in $^1$H NMR?
cards.body:
9.5

Aldehyde protons appear far downfield, typically 9-10 ppm, because of the electronegative carbonyl and its magnetic anisotropy.

Example: it often appears as a small triplet or doublet from coupling to the adjacent $\ce{CH2}$ or $\ce{CH}$.
cards.searchQuery: aldehyde proton NMR chemical shift 9-10 ppm

cards.title: Where does the O–H proton of a carboxylic acid appear in $^1$H NMR, and what does its peak look like?
cards.body:
Around 10-12 ppm, as a broad singlet.

Extensive hydrogen bonding deshields the proton strongly and exchange broadens it. Its position and width vary with concentration and solvent.

Tip: this proton disappears on shaking the sample with $\ce{D2O}$.
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid OH NMR 10-12 ppm broad singlet

cards.title: Approximately what chemical shift (ppm) do benzene ring protons show in $^1$H NMR?
cards.body:
7

Aromatic protons appear near 6.5-8.0 ppm (benzene itself is 7.3). The ring current from the delocalized π electrons strongly **deshields** them.

Example: vinyl H appear lower, around 4.5-6.5 ppm.
cards.searchQuery: aromatic proton NMR chemical shift 7 ppm ring current

cards.title: How many signals does 2-methylbutane show in its $^{13}$C NMR spectrum?
cards.body:
4

The two methyls on C2 are equivalent, so the five carbons give four environments: those two methyls, the CH, the $\ce{CH2}$, and the terminal $\ce{CH3}$.

Tip: count symmetry-distinct carbons; equivalent carbons share one signal.
cards.searchQuery: 13C NMR number of signals 2-methylbutane symmetry

cards.title: How many $^{13}$C NMR signals does 1,4-dichlorobenzene show?
cards.body:
2

Its symmetry makes the two C–Cl carbons equivalent and the four C–H carbons equivalent.

Watch out: ortho- and meta-dichlorobenzene give 3 and 4 signals respectively.
cards.searchQuery: 1,4-dichlorobenzene 13C NMR two signals symmetry

cards.title: Which has its protons farther downfield (higher ppm): $\ce{CH3F}$ or $\ce{CH3Cl}$?
cards.body:
CH3F

More electronegative atoms pull electron density away from nearby H, **deshielding** them. $\ce{CH3F}$ appears near 4.3 ppm and $\ce{CH3Cl}$ near 3.0 ppm.

Key idea: more deshielding means a higher chemical shift (downfield).
cards.searchQuery: NMR deshielding electronegativity chemical shift CH3F CH3Cl

cards.title: What happens to the O–H or N–H signal in a $^1$H NMR spectrum after adding a drop of $\ce{D2O}$?
cards.body:
It disappears (or shrinks).

The labile proton exchanges with deuterium, and $^2$H is invisible in a $^1$H spectrum. C–H signals are unaffected.

Tip: this is the standard test for identifying exchangeable protons.
cards.searchQuery: D2O shake NMR exchangeable OH NH proton disappears

cards.title: Where does a ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon appear in $^{13}$C NMR, compared with an ester or acid carbonyl?
cards.body:
Ketones and aldehydes: about 190-220 ppm. Acids, esters and amides: about 160-185 ppm.

The carbonyl carbon is the **most downfield** signal in most spectra.

Tip: a peak near 200 ppm means aldehyde or ketone; near 170 ppm means an acid derivative.
cards.searchQuery: 13C NMR carbonyl chemical shift ketone 200 ester 170

cards.title: What is the chemical shift (ppm) assigned to tetramethylsilane (TMS), the standard NMR reference?
cards.body:
0

All shifts are measured relative to TMS. Its twelve equivalent H (and four equivalent C) are highly **shielded**, so most organic signals appear downfield of it.

Example: $\ce{Si(CH3)4}$ gives a single sharp peak defined as 0 ppm.
cards.searchQuery: TMS tetramethylsilane NMR reference 0 ppm
